title: Texas Governor-Elect Hinojosa Says She Will Rescind Abbott's H-1B Hiring Freeze
excerpt: The Democrat told The Texas Tribune the freeze on new H-1B petitions at state agencies and public universities "does not make sense" — but it stays in force until she takes office on January 19.
body:
• Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune she will rescind Governor Greg Abbott’s freeze on new H-1B petitions at state agencies and public universities: “Yeah, that does not make sense to me.”
  • The freeze, imposed by Abbott’s January 27 letter, bars covered institutions from filing new H-1B petitions without written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission and runs until May 31, 2027.
  • Nothing changes until Hinojosa takes office on January 19: the freeze stays in force, and it does not cover private employers, while renewals are not treated as new petitions under commission guidance.
  • For Indian professionals, the affected jobs are at Texas public universities, medical schools and state agencies — federal H-1B eligibility itself is untouched by either the freeze or its promised reversal.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will reverse Governor Greg Abbott’s freeze on new H-1B petitions at state agencies and public universities, a change that would reopen hiring of foreign professionals — a programme widely used by Indian-born workers — across Texas public higher education and state government. Asked by The Texas Tribune whether she would rescind the restriction, Hinojosa replied: “Yeah, that does not make sense to me,” according to an IANS report of the interview published on Wednesday. “I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do,” she said.

“I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do.”

— Gina Hinojosa, Texas Governor-elect, to The Texas Tribune

Who the freeze covers — and who it does not

Abbott imposed the restriction in a January 27 letter covering state agencies controlled by gubernatorially appointed heads and public institutions of higher education. It prevents those institutions from initiating or filing new H-1B petitions without written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission until May 31, 2027, the end of the Texas Legislature’s next regular session. In the governor’s announcement, Abbott argued that taxpayer-funded employment should prioritise Texans and said the pause would give lawmakers time to establish safeguards. His directive also required covered institutions to report their existing H-1B sponsorships, workers’ countries of origin, job descriptions and recruitment efforts to the commission by March 27.

The restriction is not a blanket prohibition on every H-1B filing. Texas State University, quoting commission guidance, said renewals are not treated as new petitions requiring written approval, and the guidance also excludes changes of status for students or recent graduates of Texas higher education institutions who are already in the United States when they apply — including qualifying changes from F-1 student or J-1 exchange-visitor status to H-1B status. Private-sector employers were never covered: the freeze binds only Texas public employers, and neither it nor its reversal changes federal H-1B eligibility or grants anyone a visa.

What Hinojosa said, and the reaction

Hinojosa, a labour lawyer, also criticised abuses of the programme. Drawing on her experience, she said she opposed companies receiving job-related tax incentives and then using the money to hire H-1B workers. She cited school districts’ reliance on overseas teachers while arguing that Texas should develop a stronger pool of qualified teachers within the state; Abbott’s January letter names state agencies and public higher education institutions and does not list school districts. The H-1B answer was one of several Abbott-era measures she told the Tribune she plans to undo, among them a directive to identify public lands for migrant detention.

Immigration advocacy organisation FWD.us welcomed her position on Thursday. “This sweeping ban is hurting all Texans, not helping them,” said Zaira Garcia, its regional government relations director, arguing that restrictions on international recruitment impede public institutions’ work in education, healthcare and research.

When it changes, and what to do meanwhile

Hinojosa defeated Abbott on November 3, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990 and the state’s first Latina governor. She takes office on January 19. Until she is sworn in, Abbott’s orders remain in effect, including the H-1B freeze. For an Indian professional weighing a post at a Texas public university, medical school or state agency, the practical position is unchanged for now: a new petition from such an employer still needs written commission permission, renewals proceed under the existing guidance, and the earliest the promised rescission can take effect is her first days in office in January.
